events.title: Exhibitor Move Out
EI Before AI: The Importance of Human Connection in an AI World
events.original: Donna Housman. EI Before AI: The Importance of Human Connection in an AI World
events.gridNote: Internal schedule lists room Event Center
events.description:
Every AI decision a district makes can be judged by one question: Will this increase or decrease the quality of human interaction in our schools?
Clinical psychologist, Dr. Donna Housman, shows why the answer depends on emotional intelligence (EI). Why EI built in the first eight years and protected in every grade that follows establishes the foundation for a child’s sense of agency and builds resilience in an AI world. She makes the case that the process must start with the adults first. How investing in the wellbeing of the educators makes a critical difference in children’s success both in learning and in life. 
EI Before AI is not a ban and not a delay tactic. It is a leadership stance that recognizes the need to invest in human relationships and prioritizes and nurtures children's capacity to think clearly, connect deeply and use any tool with intention.

events.title: How Not to AI-Proof Your Classroom: Rethinking Teaching in the Age of AI
events.original: Anderson, Eileen. How Not to AI-Proof Your Classroom: Rethinking Teaching in the Age of AI
events.description:
As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in education, educators face a critical choice: attempt to control it or rethink their practice entirely. This session challenges the impulse to “AI‑proof” assignments and instead invites educators to reimagine teaching and learning. There is no AI problem, but long-standing issues in assessment, grading, and instructional design that AI now exposes.
Participants will examine why efforts to catch AI-driven cheating are both unsustainable and counterproductive. Instead, the session focuses on shifting toward authentic, meaningful learning experiences and valid assessments that better reflect what students know and can do.
Educators will explore how to intentionally and selectively incorporate AI into instruction, not as a replacement for teaching, but as a tool that enhances learning when used appropriately. Emphasis will be placed on modeling ethical, transparent AI use so students develop the critical thinking skills needed to evaluate AI outputs and determine when its use is appropriate.
Grounded in the understanding that AI cannot be avoided, this session encourages a mindset of adaptation, flexibility, and innovation. Participants will leave with practical strategies and a renewed perspective: if AI can do the task, it’s time to redesign the task.

events.title: From Data to Action — Turning Student Insights into Better Outcomes

events.description:

During this session, Educational Vistas will provide a walkthrough of DataMate, demonstrating how districts can bring assessment data together, identify learning gaps, monitor student progress, and give educators faster access to the information they need to make informed instructional decisions.
The Core Collaborative will then explore what happens beyond the data—sharing practical strategies for turning insights into action, strengthening instructional practices, and building a culture focused on continuous improvement and measurable student outcomes.
Attendees will learn how the combination of the right technology, meaningful data, and effective instructional practices can help districts:
· Identify student strengths and learning needs sooner
· Turn assessment results into actionable instructional insights
· Monitor student growth and progress over time
· Support data-informed instructional decisions
· Strengthen collaboration among teachers and school leaders
· Connect district data initiatives to measurable student outcomes
See the data. Understand what it means. Put it into action.

events.title: Protecting the Voices That Matter: Students, Teachers, and Their Words in an AI World
events.original: Gardy, Jaquie. Protecting the Voices That Matter: Students, Teachers, and Their Words in an AI World
events.description:
AI tools are now woven into the daily work of teachers and students, but few fully understand what happens to the writing, ideas, and creative work we upload. In this session, we'll explore the hidden story of what we are feeding AI systems and the real implications for intellectual property, student privacy, and long‑term digital footprints.
Drawing on my work in global education, editorial clarity, and learning design, this session brings a grounded, human‑centered perspective to a rapidly evolving landscape. We'll unpack what actually gets stored, trained on, or discarded when educators paste lesson plans, assessments, reflections, or even entire manuscripts into AI tools. Participants will examine how different platforms handle user data, how these practices impact equity and bias, and how international approaches to AI governance are shaping the future of educational technology.
But this is not a fear‑based session. We'll also explore how AI can be a powerful partner for clarity, differentiation, and workflow-when used safely and intentionally. Through short demonstrations using non‑sensitive text, we'll look at how AI can help rewrite confusing directions, generate rubrics, or improve instructional clarity without compromising creative ownership.
Educators will learn the practical differences between tools that store data, tools that train on data, and tools that discard data entirely. We'll break down how to read terms of service without being a lawyer, what teachers and students should never upload, and how to protect drafts, book ideas, curriculum materials, and other original writing.
Participants will leave with a simple, memorable framework for evaluating any AI tool:
The 3 Questions to Ask Before Using AI:
Where does my data go?
Who can see it?
Does this tool learn from what I upload?
We'll close with a hopeful, human‑centered call to action: AI is a literacy, not a threat. Students deserve to understand how their creative work is used. Teachers deserve tools that respect their intellectual property. And schools deserve clear, responsible guidance for navigating this moment.

events.title: Embracing the Future: AI as a Catalyst for Connected Learning Ecosystems
events.original: Jenelle Hodges, Embracing the Future: AI as a Catalyst for Connected Learning Ecosystems. Tuoro
events.description:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping the educational landscape, challenging educators and institutions to rethink not only the tools they use, but the very nature of teaching and learning itself. As learners increasingly engage with knowledge through interconnected digital environments, educational technology is evolving from isolated classroom tools into dynamic learning ecosystems driven by networks, personalization, collaboration, and AI-supported learning pathways.
This session explores the evolution of educational technology through the lens of connectivism and emerging AI technologies. Participants will examine how learning has shifted from static, instructor-centered models toward adaptive, learner-centered ecosystems that extend beyond traditional classrooms and schedules. Topics will include generative AI, adaptive learning platforms, AI-supported collaboration, learning analytics, digital literacy, ethical AI integration, and the growing role of educators as learning architects and facilitators within connected learning environments.
Rather than focusing solely on AI tools, this session challenges participants to consider the broader instructional and systemic shifts occurring across K–12, higher education, and organizational learning spaces. Attendees will engage in discussion surrounding learner agency, personalized learning pathways, networked knowledge, and the future of educational technology in an AI-enhanced world.
Participants will leave with practical strategies and reflective frameworks for integrating AI and connected learning principles into modern educational environments while maintaining a strong focus on ethics, accessibility, human-centered design, and meaningful learner engagement.
Session Objectives:
By the end of this session, participants will be able to:
-Examine the evolution of educational technology and learning theories leading to connectivist learning environments.
-Explore current and emerging uses of AI within modern learning ecosystems.
-Analyze how AI and networked learning are transforming learner engagement, personalization, and instructional design.
-Discuss ethical considerations related to AI integration, including equity, accessibility, privacy, and digital literacy.
-Identify practical strategies for designing learner-centered, AI-enhanced educational experiences.
-Reflect on the evolving role of educators as facilitators, curators, and learning architects within connected learning systems.

events.title: What makes a great IT Director?
events.presenter: Mr. Sandy Wagner, Salvatore DeAngelo, Ed.D., Dr. Bhargav Vyas, Mr. Moses Ojeda, Mrs. Laurie Guyon
events.original: Wagner, Sandy. What makes a great IT Director?
events.description: This panel discussion, titled "What Makes a Great Director of Technology," brings together a powerhouse quartet of New York State educational leaders to dissect the evolving DNA of school technology leadership. Hosted by the Director of Network and Instructional Technology for WSWHE BOCES, the session moves beyond hardware procurement to explore the Director of Technology (DoT) as a strategic cabinet member, instructional partner, and visionary for student success. The Panelists The conversation leverages a 360-degree view of the educational ecosystem: Dr. Bhargav Vyas, Ed.D. : Assistant Superintendent for Compliance and Information Systems Laurie Guyon: Author and Lead Coordinator for Instructional Technology Programs Dr. Salvatore DeAngelo, Ed.D. : Interim K-12 Tech Director and Retired Superintendent Moses Ojeda: Principal Main Objectives The discussion is anchored by four primary goals designed to provide a roadmap for current and aspiring technology leaders: 1. Redefining the "Seat at the Table" The panel aims to transition the image of the DoT from a "fixer of things" to a "driver of strategy." Objectives include identifying how a great Director balances technical infrastructure with high-level district goals and how they build the necessary trust with Boards of Education and Superintendents to influence policy. 2. Harmonizing Innovation with Security In an era of Ed Law 2-d and rising cybersecurity threats, the session explores the "Great" Director's ability to act as a "Gate-opener" rather than a "Gatekeeper." The objective is to share strategies for maintaining a robust, compliant security posture without stifling the creative, pedagogical needs of teachers and students. 3. Operationalizing the "Portrait of a Graduate" A central pillar of the discussion is the alignment of technology with the Portrait of a Graduate framework. The panel seeks to define how a Director ensures that every fiber-optic cable and 1:1 device serves the ultimate goal: developing students who are adaptable, digitally literate, and career-ready. It moves the conversation from outputs (number of devices) to outcomes (student competencies). 4. Identifying the "X-Factor" of Leadership Beyond certifications and technical prowess, the panel aims to isolate the soft skills—emotional intelligence, crisis management, and storytelling—that differentiate a functional director from a transformational leader. The objective is to provide the audience with a "profile of excellence" for future hiring and professional development. Discussion Flow The 50-minute session is structured as a high-energy dialogue, beginning with the Evolution of the Role, moving through the IT/Instructional Divide, addressing the pressures of Compliance and AI, and culminating in a deep dive into Future-Ready Skills. It concludes with a "Lightning Round" designed to provide sharp, actionable insights on the most pressing tech-leadership debates of 2026. This session serves as both a masterclass in educational leadership and a collaborative brainstorming session for the future of New York’s digital learning landscape.explores the evolving role of school technology leadership from a technical "fixer" to a strategic, visionary cabinet member. Hosted by Sandy Wagner, the Director of Network and Instructional Technology for WSWHE BOCES, the session features a powerful lineup of New York educational leaders, including Dr. Bhargav Vyas, Laurie Guyon, Dr. Salvatore DeAngelo, and Moses Ojeda. Together, they will discuss how a great Director balances robust cybersecurity with classroom innovation, aligns infrastructure with student competencies, and utilizes essential soft skills like emotional intelligence to drive long-term district strategy.

In this interactive session, participants will explore the 3D design process while learning how elementary students can use Computer-Aided Design (CAD) to solve real-world problems connected to architecture, construction, engineering, manufacturing, and digital innovation.
Designed for educators in grades 3–5, this model lesson demonstrates how technology integration can be meaningful, accessible, and highly engaging for elementary learners. Aligned to the New York State Computer Science and Digital Fluency Standards, this session supports STEM and interdisciplinary learning while fostering creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and problem-solving skills. events.title: Come Experience this High School Science Lesson!
events.original: Robinson, Sarah. Come Live this High School Science Lesson!
events.gridTitle: Robinson, Sarah. Come Live this High School Science Lesson!
events.description: This is a fast, fun, 30-minute mission to become a Nature Detective! You will work in teams to solve a big mystery: Why are plants and animals disappearing in a New York State park? You will use a special, small computer (called a micro:bit) that has sensors to check the invisible "weather" in three different areas. You will plug in the sensors to measure light, water (moisture), and heat (temperature). Your team must hunt for this data in your assigned area, and then share your findings with the other teams. By working together, you will figure out the exact problem in each area—like if it is too hot or too dry. You will then come up with a real plan to save the park! You will learn how real scientists and engineers use technology to help nature.

events.title: Intentional Technology: Designing Screen Time That Matters
events.original: Winnick, Alana. Intentional Technology: Designing Screen Time That Matters
events.description:
As conversations about technology become increasingly focused on screen time totals, bans, and restrictions, we risk overlooking a more important question: What is technology replacing or displacing, and what is it making possible? Not all screen time is created equal. Some digital experiences promote creativity, collaboration, communication, reflection, accessibility, and deeper learning. Others simply fill time. The challenge for educators is learning how to tell the difference.
In this session, participants will explore a framework for evaluating technology through the lens of intentionality rather than minutes spent on a device. Through classroom examples, student work, real-world scenarios, and practical reflection tools, attendees will learn how to design technology experiences that enhance learning while avoiding technology use that merely digitizes existing practices. Participants will leave with a new way of thinking about technology decisions and practical strategies for creating learning experiences where technology serves a purpose rather than becoming the purpose.

events.description:
Presentation Description:
Project-Based Learning in Action: Cultivating the New York State Portrait of a Graduate Through Service, Leadership, and Real-World Learning
This interactive presentation explores how Project-Based Learning (PBL) can transform education by developing the competencies outlined in the New York State Portrait of a Graduate. Participants will discover how authentic, hands-on learning experiences foster student engagement while preparing learners to become compassionate leaders, effective communicators, innovative thinkers, and active contributors to their communities.
Drawing from more than 25 years of experience in education and educational leadership, participants will gain firsthand insight into the successful transformation of a school from a traditional New York State Regents model to a Project-Based Learning framework. Implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic, this innovative model united students, faculty, families, the Board of Trustees, community organizations, businesses, and elected officials in creating meaningful learning experiences connected to real-world challenges.
Through engaging examples and practical strategies, attendees will examine how Project-Based Learning naturally develops each component of the New York State Portrait of a Graduate by fostering:
- Academic Preparedness: Demonstrating rigor via a model that displays learning beyond the classroom using real world applications.
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving through authentic, community-based projects.
-Creative Innovator: Shared experiences with community partnerships helps the growth and development of the student in order to make an effective impact on society for the future.
-Critical Thinker: Utilizing an "essential question" to aid in problem solving skills and techniques, working collaboratively with others and giving students a voice and choice in their learning to determine what information do they want to know, what problem do they want to solve and what are the necessary steps to take in order to solve it.
-Effective Communication: by strengthening written, verbal, interpersonal, and public speaking skills students will learn and develop via life discovery interviews and public speaking opportunities in their day to day learning. This also builds a positive and meaningful culture and community both in and outside of the school via collaboration through teamwork with peers, educators, businesses, nonprofit organizations, and community leaders.
-Global Citizenship: Civic Responsibility through service-learning and partnerships that connect students to their communities. Innovation and Creativity by encouraging students to design solutions to meaningful local and global challenges. Students will take unmet needs in society to form and focus on a capstone/service project.
Reflective/Future Focused: Self-Awareness and Social-Emotional Competence by integrating reflection, mindfulness, resilience, and relationship-building into the learning process.
Leadership and Initiative by empowering students to take ownership of their learning, advocate for their ideas, and inspire positive change. Student assessments will be inclusive of journals, peer reviews and a team approach to success. Students will turnkey learning to others both in and outside of the school community.
This Lifelong Learning model will prepare students to navigate an ever-changing world with confidence, curiosity, and purpose.
Participants will leave with practical tools, project ideas, and implementation strategies that can be adapted across grade levels and content areas. The session demonstrates how Project-Based Learning serves as a powerful framework for developing not only academic achievement but also the leadership, communication, wellness, and real-world skills students need to thrive in college, careers, and life.
This presentation is ideal for educators, administrators, school counselors, instructional leaders, and community partners seeking innovative approaches to student-centered learning that align with the New York State Portrait of a Graduate while building strong school-community partnerships and preparing students to become confident, compassionate, and engaged citizens.

Through authentic classroom examples and live demonstrations, we will examine how AI can analyze exit tickets, writing samples, engineering notebooks, and formative assessments to reveal trends across an entire class, suggest targeted interventions, and draft personalized feedback that teachers review and refine.
The session will also introduce privacy-conscious approaches, including local AI models that allow student work to be analyzed entirely on a teacher's own device without sending student data to the cloud. Participants will leave with practical workflows, adaptable prompts, and a new framework for thinking about assessment as a process of collecting evidence, identifying patterns, and making informed instructional decisions. The focus is not on replacing teacher expertise, but on leveraging AI to reduce repetitive tasks, strengthen formative assessment, and give teachers more time to do what matters most: understand student thinking and support student learning.

events.title: AI as Friend, Foe, or Tool: Navigating the AI Paradox in K-12 Education
events.original: Blank, Lisa. AI as Friend, Foe, or Tool: Navigating the AI Paradox in K-12 Education
events.description:
As K-12 educators and administrators, you face mounting pressure to integrate AI into teaching and learning. This focused discussion moves beyond "embrace or ban" thinking to explore the AI paradox: how the same tool can simultaneously enhance learning and undermine critical thinking depending on implementation.
Drawing from recent research with state education leaders and students, we'll examine why AI literacy, not just AI usage, matters for today's learners. Through interactive scenarios across content areas, you'll develop practical frameworks for making context-specific decisions about AI integration that maintain academic integrity while building future-ready skills.
We'll address equity considerations across diverse student populations, explore research-backed pedagogical approaches, and share strategies from educators already navigating this complexity. Leave with concrete protocols to guide your own AI decision-making and support teachers in your school communities.
This isn't about finding the "right answer"—it's about building your agency to make sophisticated, informed choices that serve your students' best interests.
By the end of this session, participants will be able to:
Reframe the AI conversation by moving beyond binary "embrace or ban" thinking to recognize AI as a context-dependent tool that can both enhance and undermine learning.
Understand the AI paradox and articulate how the same AI application can simultaneously support and hinder critical thinking depending on how, when, and why it is implemented.
Apply a decision-making framework to evaluate AI use across different content areas and instructional contexts, using a structured before/during/after approach.
Analyze authentic classroom scenarios to practice making informed, context-specific decisions about appropriate AI integration.
Prioritize AI literacy over AI usage by recognizing that building durable decision-making skills matters more than mastering any specific tool.
Address equity considerations related to AI access and implementation across diverse student populations.
Develop actionable protocols that participants can bring back to guide their own practice and support teachers in their school communities.
Strengthen educator agency to make sophisticated, research-informed choices that serve students' best interests rather than reacting to external pressures.

events.description:
In the current NYS educational landscape, districts often struggle to balance the academic rigor of the Next Generation Learning Standards (NGLS) with the holistic vision of the Portrait of a Graduate (PoaG). This session explores how high-quality Project-Based Learning (PBL) serves as the essential bridge between these two frameworks, transforming traditional content into durable, life-ready skills. We will dive into the "how" of designing learning experiences that move beyond checking boxes to building graduates. Attendees will explore strategies for utilizing structured PBL frameworks (with varied levels of technology use)—including examples from the iBlocks model—to create flexible learning pathways that foster student agency while remaining anchored to state mandates. By examining real-world student success stories, from primary-level robotics to high-school engineering ethics, participants will gain a model for a classroom environment where standards and student identity work in tandem. Leave this session with a practical approach to ensuring every graduate is academically prepared, creatively innovative, and ready to contribute to a modern world. This interactive session is designed to provide a practical blueprint for educators and administrators seeking to align daily instruction with the New York State Portrait of a Graduate. 
The presentation is divided into three distinct phases: 
• The Alignment Framework: We begin by examining the common friction points between meeting rigorous Next Gen Standards and fostering the "durable skills" defined in the Portrait of a Graduate. Participants will explore how a well-structured PBL approach prevents these initiatives from becoming "one more thing" by merging them into a single instructional goal. 
• PBL in Action: Using real-world success stories (including examples from the iBlocks framework), we will showcase how K-12 students transition from passive learners to active contributors. We will examine specific project flows—such as 1st-grade animal advocacy through robotics, middle-school comic book narratives for social awareness, and high-school prosthetic design—to see how standards and "the graduate" coexist. 
• The Implementation Roadmap: We will conclude by providing attendees with strategies to scale these experiences across their districts, focusing on how to provide "Context for Content" so that every lesson serves a larger purpose. Main Objectives: - Identify the specific intersections where Next Generation Learning Standards (NGLS) naturally support the attributes of the NYS Portrait of a Graduate. - Analyze the "Design Challenge" flow as a pedagogical tool to develop resilience, critical thinking, and student agency across all grade levels. - Construct a plan for integrating structured PBL resources into existing curricula to ensure equitable access to high-quality, future-focused learning experiences.

events.title: Prompting Pedagogy: How Pre-Service Elementary Teachers Used AI to Design, Reflect, and Grow as Educators
events.presenter: Pamela Gleisner, Dr Gabriela Mocanu, Tiffany Thompson
events.original: Mocanu, Gabriela. Prompting Pedagogy: How Pre-Service Elementary Teachers Used AI to Design, Reflect, and Grow as Educators
events.description:
What happens when pre-service elementary teachers stop fearing artificial intelligence and start using it as a professional tool? In this hands-on workshop, participants will find out, through the real experiences, real lesson plans, and real reflections of teacher candidates who spent time doing exactly that. 
This session emerges from a practitioner research study conducted within an elementary teacher preparation program at a New York State college. Pre-service teachers preparing to work in K–6 classrooms were invited to use a range of AI tools as part of their lesson planning coursework. They were not simply handed a tool and told to produce a plan. They were asked to engage critically: to prompt, to evaluate, to revise, and to reflect on what AI could and could not do that a thoughtful educator must. What emerged was more than a collection of lesson plans. It was a window into how the next generation of teachers is making sense of one of the most consequential technologies to enter the profession in decades. 
This workshop brings that experience into the conference room. Participants will hear directly from the teacher educator and her students who designed and studied this process, and, in a format that mirrors the study itself, will have the opportunity to try AI lesson planning tools firsthand, examine sample work from pre-service teacher candidates, and engage in structured reflection about what this means for their own practice and for the programs and schools they lead. 
The session is grounded in the theme of this year's conference, Quantum Leap: Big Ideas, Real Classrooms, Bold Futures, because what this research documents is precisely that kind of leap: not a cautious, incremental experiment with technology, but a deliberate, pedagogically intentional choice to prepare future elementary teachers for the AI-integrated classrooms they are already walking into. The findings are practical, honest, and sometimes surprising. The conversation they generate is one the field urgently needs to have. 
Whether you are a teacher educator wondering how to integrate AI into your preparation program, a K–12 administrator trying to set responsible AI policies, a classroom teacher navigating AI with your own students, or a technology integrationist looking for models that actually work in real educational contexts, this session is designed for you. 
Workshop Objectives:
1. Describe how AI tools can be purposefully integrated into pre-service teacher education as a vehicle for developing pedagogical reasoning, not replacing it. Attendees will gain a clear, research-grounded picture of how one teacher preparation program structured AI use in a lesson planning context, what tools were used, how candidates were scaffolded, what was required of them critically, and what the outcomes looked like. This objective addresses a gap that many teacher educators report: not knowing how to begin, or what responsible integration actually looks like in practice. 
2. Apply educator-specific AI tools to a lesson planning task in their own content area or grade level, using a structured prompting framework developed through the research. The heart of the workshop is a hands-on experience in which participants use tools such as MagicSchool AI and/or Curipod to draft or extend a lesson plan, guided by the same prompting scaffolds given to the pre-service teachers in the study. Participants will then evaluate and discuss their output in pairs or small groups, replicating the reflective structure that made the original course experience educationally meaningful. 
4. Identify at least two implications for their own professional context, whether in teacher preparation, K–12 instruction, curriculum design, or school leadership, and articulate a concrete next step for responsible AI integration. The session closes with structured individual reflection and whole-group synthesis. Participants will leave not just with ideas but with a specific, actionable commitment: a next step they are prepared to take in their own setting. This connects the workshop's content directly to the NYSCATE mission of bold, future-ready practice in real classrooms. 
5. Engage with the ethical, pedagogical, and equity dimensions of AI in elementary teacher preparation, including questions of over-reliance, academic integrity, data privacy, and the irreplaceable human dimensions of teaching. Consistent with both the conference theme and the New York State Portrait of a Graduate's emphasis on critical thinking and ethical citizenship, this session does not present AI as a simple solution. Participants will grapple with the same tensions the pre-service teachers themselves named: when AI helps, when it misleads, and what it means to prepare young children, and their future teachers, to be thoughtful, humane participants in an AI-shaped world.

events.title: Leading AI: Brewing Innovation from Vision to Practice
events.original: Karandy, Steve. Leading AI: Brewing Innovation from Vision to Practice
events.description:
Artificial intelligence is moving faster than most school systems were designed to adapt. New tools emerge almost weekly, teachers are experimenting at different levels, students are already using AI outside of school, and district leaders are being asked to make decisions about policy, privacy, professional learning, academic integrity, and classroom practice.
The question is no longer whether AI will impact education. The question is whether school leaders will intentionally build the systems needed to lead through that change.
This session will explore what it looks like to lead AI implementation across a school district and move from isolated experimentation to a more intentional, sustainable approach. Rather than starting with the newest AI tool, leaders must begin by establishing a clear vision for how AI supports teaching, learning, efficiency, accessibility, and the district's broader instructional priorities.
Participants will examine a practical leadership framework centered on four connected areas: Vision, Professional Learning, Tools, and Systems.
Vision creates clarity around why a district is using AI and what responsible, human-centered implementation should look like to keep a "human in the loop" approach. Professional learning builds educator confidence through modeling, experimentation, coaching, and opportunities to try one practical workflow at a time. Tool selection focuses on solving real problems, reducing friction, protecting student data, and fitting within existing district ecosystems. Systems create the guardrails, routines, communication structures, and leadership support necessary for innovation to move beyond a handful of early adopters.
Through real examples of district implementation, participants will explore how AI tools can support educator efficiency, differentiation, feedback, accessibility, and student learning. The session will also address the challenges leaders must navigate, including data privacy, academic integrity, AI literacy, uneven staff readiness, tool overload, and the temptation to create policies based primarily on fear.
A central theme of the session is that AI implementation is a leadership challenge before it is a technology challenge. Schools cannot simply provide access to AI and expect meaningful change. Leaders must model responsible use, create safe opportunities for experimentation, communicate clear expectations, listen to educator feedback, and be willing to adjust when an initiative is not working as intended.
Participants will also examine the growing importance of AI literacy. Access to AI tools is not enough. Students and educators must learn how AI works, how to question its outputs, recognize limitations and bias, protect personal information, verify information, and determine when AI should or should not be used. The goal is not to create better prompt writers, but to develop better thinkers who can work alongside emerging technology with judgment, creativity, and integrity.
This session is designed for superintendents, district administrators, principals, instructional technology leaders, curriculum leaders, and other educators responsible for guiding AI implementation. Participants will leave with a practical framework they can adapt to their own organization, examples of AI implementation in practice, and clear next steps for moving their district from AI experimentation toward intentional leadership.
AI will continue to change. The tools will evolve. The platforms we use today may look completely different in the future. Strong leadership, however, remains the constant.
The work of leading AI is not about predicting every change or chasing every new tool. It is about building a culture that stays curious, develops clear guardrails, learns through experimentation, and keeps human judgment at the center.
It is time to stop waiting for the perfect AI roadmap and start building the leadership systems that allow schools to learn, adapt, and innovate with purpose.

And where did that come from?! Along the way, we’ll explore digital footprints, AI-generated assumptions, privacy, and the trail we leave behind online. events.title: The Vibe Coding Quantum Leap: Coding at the Speed of Thought for Tomorrow’s Innovators
events.original: Roberto, Dan. The Vibe Coding Quantum Leap: Coding at the Speed of Thought for Tomorrow’s Innovators
events.description:
"Vibe coding" shifts software development from complex programming syntax to simple, natural-language conversations with AI. Because users can build fully functional web apps, tools, and simulations using everyday speech, this game-changing technology is instantly accessible to every teacher and student, zero coding experience required.
Grounded in the core tenets of Universal Design for Learning (UDL), this high-energy session demonstrates how educators can use a cutting-edge workflow (Gemini Canvas, Claude, and Canva Code) to rapidly engineer personalized, curriculum-aligned digital environments on the fly. No longer bound by rigid, off-the-shelf software templates, teachers can build custom tools tailored precisely to their instructional vision and student needs.
Beyond teacher customization, we will explore how shifting this creative power to students directly actualizes New York State’s new Portrait of a Graduate framework. By lowering technical barriers, vibe coding turns learners into digital architects. You will discover practical, classroom-tested frameworks that empower students to act as Creative Innovators who rapidly prototype real-world solutions, Critical Thinkers who debug logic systems, and Effective Communicators who leverage multiple means of expression to share their mastery.
Participants will walk away with an immediate classroom action plan to leverage Gemini, Claude and Canva Code to natively publish student-designed tools. Leave this session equipped with the actionable strategies needed to execute a literal quantum leap in your district, transitioning classrooms from passive tech consumption to high-velocity, hyper-personalized creation.
Main Objectives:
Master the Vibe-Coding Ecosystem: Learn to utilize Gemini Canvas, Claude, and Canva Code to build functional web tools with zero traditional coding experience.
Design Personalized UDL Scaffolds: Instantly materialize an instructional vision into custom, curriculum-aligned digital simulators and interactive resources tailored to diverse student learning profiles.
Activate the Portrait of a Graduate: Acquire a practical classroom blueprint that turns students into digital architects, empowering them to act as Creative Innovators, Critical Thinkers, and Effective Communicators by vibe-coding their own real-world solutions.

events.title: Maturing Your Cybersecurity Posture—Scoping, Implementing, and Actionizing Penetration Testing
events.original: Wagner, Casey. Maturing Your Cybersecurity Posture—Scoping, Implementing, and Actionizing Penetration Testing
events.description:
Are you ready to strengthen your school district’s cybersecurity posture? This dynamic session offers actionable insights into using penetration testing to drive meaningful improvements in education environments. Discover how collaborative leadership and technical expertise can transform your district’s approach to cyber threats. Learn how to effectively scope, conduct, and leverage penetration test results to ensure your systems, staff, and students are protected. Join me and empower your district to move from reactive defenses to proactive resilience.
•Context & Challenge: K-12 school districts are increasingly targeted by sophisticated cyber threats. With limited resources and ever-evolving attack vectors, it’s crucial to apply rigorous assessment methods—akin to those used for instructional improvement—to the realm of cybersecurity.
•Session Approach: This session brings together the unique perspectives of a Director of Technology who has led district-wide cybersecurity initiatives and a CEO with deep expertise in penetration testing for educational institutions. Together, they will illustrate how to build district-level support for penetration testing, highlighting leadership strategies, technical requirements, and budget considerations.
•Scoping Best Practices: Participants will learn how to define objectives, select appropriate testing methodologies, and set realistic expectations tailored for K-12 environments. The presenters will discuss how to identify critical assets, prioritize risk areas, and ensure compliance with data privacy regulations.
•Implementation Insights: Gain behind-the-scenes perspectives on partnering with external experts, preparing staff and systems for testing, and managing logistical challenges unique to schools. Real-world anecdotes from both district and vendor sides will demystify the process.
•Actionizing Results: The session will move beyond testing to focus on translating findings into practical improvements. Strategies for communicating results to stakeholders, integrating remediation into existing workflows, and developing ongoing improvement plans will be shared. Special attention will be given to post-assessment support and building a culture of cyber resilience.
Outcomes: Attendees will leave with a toolkit of strategies to mature their district’s cybersecurity posture, actionable steps for implementing penetration testing, and a framework for continuous improvement and stakeholder engagement.

events.title: NYSDLC - The World Is Waiting: A Global Mystery Connection
events.original: NYSDLC. Edwards, Kristin. The World Is Waiting: A Global Mystery Connection.
events.gridTitle: NYSDLC. Edwards, Kristin. The World Is Waiting: A Global Mystery Connection.
events.description:
Be a world traveler—no passport required! Join us for a live global connection as we partner with a class somewhere in the world and play "Geography 20 Questions" (often called "Mystery Skype"). Using only yes/no questions, you'll work together to uncover your partner class's location while they try to find yours. But that's just the beginning. Once you've found each other, the real magic happens: authentic conversations about daily life, culture, traditions, school, community, weather, hopes, challenges, and experiences. These powerful human-to-human connections help break down stereotypes, build understanding, and foster empathy—something our world needs now more than ever. Experience firsthand how technology can transform a classroom into a window to the world, and imagine the possibilities for your own students.
Participants will:
*Experience a live global classroom connection from the learner's perspective.
*Explore how technology can be used to create authentic learning experiences beyond the walls of the classroom.
*Recognize the role global collaboration can play in developing empathy, cultural awareness, perspective-taking, and communication skills.
*Identify ways that global connections support the "social curriculum" and help prepare students to thrive in an increasingly interconnected world.
*Discover practical opportunities and resources for bringing virtual global collaborations into their own schools and classrooms.
*Reflect on how authentic human connections can help break down stereotypes, foster understanding, and build a greater sense of global citizenship among students.

events.title: Can I Have Your Attention, Please? Creating Captivating Presentations
events.original: Bond. Virgina. Can I Have Your Attention, Please? Creating Captivating Presentations
events.description:
"Can I have your attention, please?!" If you are tired of watching your audience glaze over and check their phones, it’s time to rebuild your presentations from the nuts and bolts up! Join Mike Doughty and Virginia Bond for a high-energy, fast-paced ride through the complete life cycle of an unforgettable presentation.
We will show you exactly how to hack adult learning styles so your audience stays awake, stays connected, and actually remembers your message. You'll discover the secrets to confidently working the room like a seasoned pro, using physical space and pacing to command the stage and eliminate podium fatigue.
Plus, we are pulling back the curtain on how to team up with generative AI assistants to handle the tedious, non-technical layout tasks—making your slide design look effortless while saving you hours of prep time. Whether you are pitching a new initiative, leading a faculty workshop, or presenting under the big lights, don't just give another boring speech. Learn to own your presence, optimize your workflow, and walk away with real, measurable results!

events.title: The REAL ROI of Connection: How 100% Device Return was Only the Start
events.original: Hacker, Daniel. The REAL ROI of Connection: How 100% Device Return was Only the Start
events.description:
Picture a 100% senior device returned at one high school, and 98% of library materials recovered for a middle school. For most districts that sounds impossible. But that’s just the beginning of the value Dan Hacker, Teacher Trainer for Instructional Technology, has found with his school-to-family engagement model. The real ROI goes beyond cost savings: staff satisfaction improves when no longer having to do the tedious work of chasing families and students down for information, teachers able to focus on teaching, and the entire school community is active and engaged. Attendees will leave with an ROI action plan for getting more from their technology infrastructure to save, create value, and drive parent and student engagement. 
Dan has led this work across multiple communities: consolidate the channels, set a predictable cadence, translate automatically, and open genuine two-way conversation. In this session he’ll take attendees through each step: the problem, staff resistance to change and the rollout and implementation that earned buy-in. 
This transformation extends beyond the parent engagement to show how it also addresses the upcoming New York State Portrait of a Graduate mandate. He will share how bringing students into the same system turns passive notification into an active digital literacy lab. By using the platform to manage their own school lives, students build and document the exact proficiencies in effective communication, digital citizenship, and self-regulation that the state framework requires.

This session addresses the fundamental challenge of defining authentic technology integration beyond mere buzzwords. We will explore several critical inquiries: What defines high-impact instructional technology in practice? How do we determine the optimal balance between students' online and offline cognitive activities? Furthermore, how can we effectively articulate these pedagogical shifts to our teachers, students, and the broader community? To provide actionable frameworks, we will conduct a critical analysis of the SAMR, TPACK, and Triple E integration models, evaluating their practical application within our unique school environments.

events.title: Are We Preparing Students for the World They’re Actually Going to Enter?
events.original: Stacy, Gabriel. Are We Preparing Students for the World They’re Actually Going to Enter? Acture
events.description: The students sitting in today's classrooms will enter a workforce transformed by artificial intelligence, automation, and technologies that haven't even been invented yet. We can try to predict which jobs will exist ten years from now—but history suggests we'll probably get some of those predictions wrong.

events.title: Experience Computer Science & AI Literacy with LEGO® Education
events.presenter: Alexa Hirschberg, Joseph Sanfilippo, Caitlin Boline
events.original: SanFlippo, Joe. Experience Computer Science & AI Literacy with LEGO® Education. Lego 2
events.description: Join the LEGO® Education team as we explore how Computer Science & AI kits empower educators to bring computer science, artificial intelligence, and computational thinking to life through engaging, hands-on learning experiences. Discover how to help students build confidence, develop problem-solving skills, and deepen their understanding through purposeful inquiry-based instruction. In this interactive session, participants will learn how this work aligns to the NYS Portrait of a Graduate profile while introducing students to coding, robotics, data literacy, AI concepts, and real-world engineering design challenges. Learn practical strategies for integrating computer science and AI across grade levels to inspire the next generation of innovators.

events.title: Come experience this 4th grade STEAM lesson!
events.original: Sylor, Julie. Come live this 4th grade STEAM lesson!
events.gridTitle: Sylor, Julie. Come live this 4th grade STEAM lesson!
events.description:
Experience an engaging, hands-on STEAM lesson that brings creativity, engineering, and computer science to life through 3D design with Tinkercad! In this interactive session, participants will explore the 3D design process while learning how elementary students can use Computer-Aided Design (CAD) to solve real-world problems connected to architecture, construction, engineering, manufacturing, and digital innovation.
Designed for educators in grades 3–5, this model lesson demonstrates how technology integration can be meaningful, accessible, and highly engaging for elementary learners. Participants will leave with practical strategies, classroom-ready ideas, and confidence in teaching foundational CAD concepts—even with little or no prior experience.
Aligned to the New York State Computer Science and Digital Fluency Standards, this session supports STEM and interdisciplinary learning while fostering creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and problem-solving skills. Best of all, no 3D printer is required! Teachers will discover how students can fully engage in authentic engineering design challenges using free digital tools and design-thinking practices, making this lesson adaptable for any classroom setting.
Whether you are new to STEAM instruction or looking to expand your technology toolbox, this session will inspire you to bring innovative, student-centered learning experiences into your classroom.

events.title: Come Experience this kindergarten lesson!
events.original: DiMarino, Kara. Come Experience this Kindergarten Lesson.
events.description: Step into the role of a Kindergarten learner in this hands-on session exploring how Clixo can support problem-based learning, design thinking, and computational thinking. Working with a partner, participants will design a freestanding structure that creates a shady resting spot for a small figurine. Through a simple “Plan, Build, Try, Change” cycle, they will investigate light and shadow, develop a shared plan, follow picture-based testing steps, compare two designs, and use observations to improve their creation. Designed for children ages 4–6 and aligned with NYS engineering design and computer science standards, the lesson emphasizes collaboration, purposeful play, and explaining how a design meets a need.

events.title: Build a Better Start: Replace Bell Ringers With Tasks That Actually Think
events.original: Thomas, Dan. Build a Better Start: Replace Bell Ringers With Tasks That Actually Think
events.description:
The bell ringer isn't a warm-up. It's a signal. And right now, most bell ringers are signaling the wrong thing.
Sit down. Get quiet. Wait for me. That's what a worksheet on the board communicates before class even starts. A thinking task communicates something completely different: this is your room, your thinking matters, and we start without me. Same first five minutes. Completely different classroom.
This session makes one focused argument — replace one passive warm-up with one thinking task that puts cognitive work on students from the moment they walk in. Not a unit redesign. Not a new curriculum. Just the first five minutes.
Participants will experience three bell ringer thinking tasks as learners — each one short, subject-agnostic, and immediately accessible. Then they'll analyze what made each one work: it activated prior knowledge without reviewing it, surfaced a misconception without correcting it, and set up the lesson's core idea without revealing it.
Participants then pull out one upcoming lesson and build their own thinking task opener using a three-question design check: Does this require thinking or just recall? Could a student answer this without engaging with the content? Does this open a door or close one?
Objectives: (1) Experience three thinking task openers as a learner. (2) Identify the design moves that make a task generative. (3) Build one bell ringer thinking task ready for Monday. (4) Apply a three-question design check to future warm-ups.

events.title: Beyond the Prompt: Authentic Learning with AI in the School Library
events.original: Penn, Laura. Beyond the Prompt: Authentic Learning with AI in the School Library
events.description:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming education, but its greatest potential lies beyond generating answers. In this session, discover how AI can serve as a catalyst for authentic learning experiences that empower students to create, collaborate, think critically, and engage deeply with content.
Through real-world examples from an active school library program, participants will explore how AI-enhanced tools are being used to support student-created book trailers, digital storytelling, reading promotion campaigns, makerspace projects, cultural programming, and multimedia design experiences. Rather than focusing solely on the technology itself, this session highlights how AI can amplify student voice, foster creativity, and support meaningful learning outcomes across grade levels and content areas.
Attendees will leave with practical strategies, project ideas, and implementation tips for integrating AI into library and classroom experiences in ways that build digital literacy, strengthen durable skills, and connect learning to authentic audiences. Whether you are just beginning your AI journey or looking to expand existing initiatives, this session will provide actionable ideas for transforming students from consumers of information into creators of knowledge.

events.title: Kira: An AI-Native Operating System to Measure Portrait of a Graduate Growth
events.original: Sanducci, Chloe. Kira: An AI-Native Operating System to Measure Portrait of a Graduate Growth. Kira.
events.description: NY Inspires moves New York past Regents exams as a graduation requirement, which means districts will need to show how every student is growing on both the standards and the Portrait of a Graduate. Adding one more AI tool is an incremental upgrade, and it means another vendor to vet under Ed Law 2-d, another integration to maintain, and more data that never connects. This session makes the case for a bigger leap: one AI-native operating system for instruction, with curriculum, personalized learning, assessment, and mastery data in one place. You'll see how Kira turns that connected data into evidence of academic readiness and critical thinking for every student, and hear early results from Kira partners. Then you'll map your own district's tools to find where data connects and where it breaks, and leave with a starting plan for tracking one Portrait attribute.

events.title: AI Governance for K12 Leaders: From AI Experimentation to Responsible Adoption
events.original: Finn, Dorsey. AI Governance for K12 Leaders: From AI Experimentation to Responsible Adoption. Shi Diamond Sponsor
events.description: A vendor-agnostic framework for K-12 AI governance. Learn why policy alone isn't governance, how to choose a governance model that fits your district's capacity, and how to evaluate any AI use through purpose, users, data, impact, and human oversight.

events.title: Did You See That? AR & VR in the Classroom
events.original: Jenn Hall. Did You See That? AR & VR in the Classroom
events.description: Ready to bring a new dimension to your lessons? Step into the world of Augmented and Virtual Reality and discover how these powerful tools can captivate every student. This session will immerse you in innovative ways to boost engagement using AR and VR experiences, including exciting content creation ideas. You’ll leave with a toolbox of easy-to-use apps, resources, and practical ideas for incorporating immersive learning into your standards-based curriculum. Get ready to transform your classroom into a portal of possibilities!

events.title: AI in the Quantum Era: Transforming K-12 education for Future-Ready Learners
events.original: Needles, Tim. AI in the Quantum Era: Transforming K-12 education for Future-Ready Learners
events.description:
Right now, your students are living in the dawn of the Generative AI era. They are learning to prompt, create, and think alongside machine learning models that process information using standard, binary computer chips. But while the educational world works hard to adapt to this current wave of artificial intelligence, an even more disruptive revolution is quietly gathering speed behind the scenes: Quantum Computing.
As educators, technology leaders, and innovators, we want to understand what's coming and the New York State investment in Quantum. We are rapidly approaching a monumental tipping point where standard computer processors will no longer be fast enough or powerful enough to handle the sheer volume of data our world generates. Enter the quantum era. By harnessing the mind-bending laws of quantum mechanics, these next-generation systems process information in ways that defy classical logic. When you combine this exponential computing power with the cognitive capabilities of artificial intelligence, the result isn't just an upgrade, it’s an entirely new technological species. Quantum-Enhanced AI will fundamentally reshape human capability, transforming everything from global cybersecurity and climate forecasting to how our students will learn, work, and live.
This high-energy, forward-looking session is designed specifically to strip away the intimidating academic jargon and make the future of technology entirely accessible to the K-12 community. You don’t need a degree in advanced physics or data science to attend. Instead, we will break down the core pillars of quantum mechanics, like superposition and entanglement, into clear, brilliant visual analogies that you can easily take back to your students.

events.title: State Ed Update from the Department of Educational Design & Technology
events.original: Cardentino, Paul. StateEd UPdate!
events.gridTitle: Cardentino, Paul. StateEd UPdate!
events.description: Join the New York State Education Department's Coordinator of Educational Design and Technology for an informative session highlighting the latest updates, initiatives, and priorities impacting educational technology across New York State. Gain insights into emerging trends, state-level guidance, and ongoing efforts to support innovative teaching and learning. This session will provide educators, administrators, and technology leaders with valuable information to help align their district practices with New York State's evolving educational technology landscape.

events.title: The Education Threat Landscape: Insights from the Threat Observatory
events.original: Brown, Julian. The Education Threat Landscape: Insights from the Threat Observatory. Lumu Technologies.
events.description:
Educational institutions continue to be among the most targeted sectors by cybercriminals, facing an evolving mix of ransomware, credential theft, phishing, and malware campaigns. But beyond the headlines, what do real-world compromises reveal about how attackers operate?
Drawing on original research from the Lumu Threat Observatory, this session presents exclusive findings on the threats actively targeting K–12 schools, colleges, and universities. Attendees will gain insight into the most prevalent attack techniques, emerging adversary trends, malware activity, and indicators of compromise observed across educational environments.
Beyond presenting the data, the session translates these findings into practical guidance for security leaders, helping them prioritize defenses, improve detection, and strengthen cyber resilience based on observed attacker behavior rather than assumptions or industry anecdotes.

events.title: Beyond the Bus: Virtual Field Trips That Spark Curiosity
events.original: NYSDLC. Ross-Kleinmann, Julianne. Beyond the Bus: Virtual Field Trips That Spark Curiosity
events.description: Field trips don't have to end at the edge of your school district. Discover how the New York State Distance Learning Consortium (NYSDLC) can be your partner in expanding access by connecting students with museums, national parks, scientists, authors, classrooms, and experts around the world. Step into a virtual field trip from the learner's perspective while exploring free resources, collaborative opportunities, and practical strategies for designing engaging, standards-aligned experiences. Learn how to spark curiosity before the journey, foster active participation during the visit, and extend student thinking through reflection and creation. You'll leave with a simple planning framework, ready-to-use resources, and ideas that build communication, collaboration, critical thinking, and global awareness—helping every student connect with authentic opportunities.

events.title: Critical Creativity in Action: 10 Rapid‑Fire Strategies to Supercharge Engagement & Literacy
events.original: Ryder, Dan. Critical Creativity in Action: 10 Rapid‑Fire Strategies to Supercharge Engagement & Literacy
events.description:
What if students could choreograph a concept, pixelate a problem, or map‑make for meaning—while strengthening authentic literacy skills? Critical creativity invites learners to demonstrate understanding through purposeful making, expressive thinking, and the application of content knowledge in fresh, memorable ways.
In this fast‑paced, hands‑on session, participants will rotate through ten high‑impact strategies drawn from the Critical Creativity framework. Each strategy blends creative expression with rigorous thinking, giving educators practical tools to deepen comprehension, spark engagement, and support student voice across K–12, higher education, and professional learning environments.

This session outlines how CTOs can lead their districts out of a crisis and into a more secure future. Discover how to use NIST guidelines, risk assessments, and dedicated security teams to mitigate future threats, rebuild community trust, and fortify your network from the classroom to the central office.

events.title: Downhome Tech Sampler: A Bite-Sized Taste of EdTech
events.original: Faubs, Farmer. Downhome Tech Sampler: A Bite-Sized Taste of EdTech
events.description: Pull up a seat and dig in to this fast-paced, hands-on session designed to serve up small bites of powerful EdTech tools. Each tool is presented in a quick 5-minute overview to highlight key features, followed by a 5-minute “Taste Test” where educators get to try it out for themselves. Whether you’re new to EdTech or just looking for fresh flavor in your instruction, this sampler is designed to be approachable, engaging, and immediately useful. events.description: Move from a useful prompt to a reusable agent. events.title: Privacy and AI for Administrators
events.original: Pierce, Jill. Privacy and AI for Administrators
events.description:
As artificial intelligence and digital tools become increasingly embedded in school operations, administrators must balance efficiency with responsibility. This session focuses on how school and district leaders can leverage AI and technology to work more efficiently—streamlining communication, data analysis, and daily workflows—while safeguarding student information and maintaining FERPA compliance.
Participants will explore practical use cases for AI in administrative settings, common privacy risks, and key FERPA considerations related to student data access, sharing, and storage. Through real‑world examples and best practices, attendees will gain guidance on making informed decisions that improve productivity without compromising data security or trust. Leaders will leave with actionable strategies to support ethical, compliant, and effective technology use across their schools and districts.

events.title: Come experience a kindergarten lesson!
events.original: Closinski, Emily. Come experience a kindergarten lesson!
events.description: This lesson integrates critical thinking, literacy, and robotics in a fun, engaging way. Students begin by solving a riddle to identify a specific American symbol, which activates their problem-solving skills. They then use a grid, marked with various symbols, as their map. Their task is to program a BeeBot to navigate from its starting point to the correct symbol, using the least amount of steps possible. This challenges them to think strategically about efficient path-planning and reinforces their understanding of sequencing and directional commands. The lesson is a clever blend of social studies and computational thinking, making learning both hands-on and meaningful.

events.title: Come Experience this 6th grade lesson!

events.description:
Step into the role of a top-secret investigator in this exciting mystery adventure! A prized bag of candy has been stolen, and it’s up to students to crack the case before the trail goes cold. Using critical thinking, problem-solving, and code-breaking skills, students will decode five secret messages that reveal important clues about the crime. Each solved puzzle brings them one step closer to uncovering the suspect and solving the mystery!
This engaging activity combines teamwork, logic, and fun while encouraging students to think like real detectives. Will they solve the case before time runs out?

events.title: Esports from Nothing: Building a Successful Esports Program from Zero
events.original: Herr, Jon. Esports from Nothing: Building a Successful Esports Program from Zero
events.description:
Esports isn’t dying — not even close. Every year it grows, evolves, and becomes more impressive than the last. Join Cortland Head Coach Jon Herr, student leader Cylan Southwick, and Tech Specialist Jason Beauvais as they break down exactly how to design, pitch, recruit for, and run a successful esports program from absolutely zero. We’ll cover topics ranging from statewide programs, the tech you actually need, the real challenges of running competitive games in a school environment, and what it takes to work with (and sometimes around) a traditional Athletics department.
We hope to feature insights from groups including NYSCATE partners ELITE, ESSEFF, PlayVS, and more — because building a successful program takes a village and a whole lot of passion!

events.title: From Passive to Powerful in Practice: Designing Creative Classrooms that Work
events.original: Brooks, Kristen. From Passive to Powerful in Practice: Designing Creative Classrooms that Work
events.description: In a world where distraction is constant, transforming student device use requires more than a mindset shift it requires intentional design. This hands-on session aligned to the Spotlight Presentation, moves beyond the theme to provide educators with practical strategies for turning passive consumption into purposeful creation. Participants will explore how to redesign lessons, integrate creative tools, and implement structures that increase student engagement, improve behavior, and support self-regulation. Walk away with ready-to-use ideas, a redesigned lesson or activity, and a clear plan for putting powerful, student-centered learning into practice immediately.

events.title: More Than Coding: Finding Computational Thinking in Everyday Instruction
events.original: Pisto, Marina. More Than Coding: Finding Computational Thinking in Everyday Instruction
events.description:
Many elementary educators assume that computer science requires additional instructional time, specialized programs, or dedicated coding lessons. In reality, computational thinking is already embedded in many of the literacy, mathematics, science, and social studies experiences students encounter every day.
In this interactive session, participants will explore how foundational computational thinking concepts such as algorithms, sequencing, decomposition, pattern recognition, branching, and debugging can be developed through familiar classroom practices and unplugged learning experiences. Drawing on examples from second and third grade classrooms, presenters will demonstrate how computational thinking can be introduced through STEM centers and screen-free robotics experiences and then extended into content-area instruction through writing, reading comprehension, mathematical problem solving, scientific inquiry, and social studies investigations.
Through hands-on challenges, collaborative discussion, and analysis of authentic classroom examples, participants will identify computational thinking practices already present within their curriculum and discover practical ways to make them more visible and intentional. Attendees will engage in brief unplugged activities, examine student learning experiences, and consider how these approaches support both content-area learning and New York State Computer Science and Digital Fluency standards.
Participants will leave with ready-to-use strategies, cross-curricular lesson ideas, and a framework for embedding computational thinking into existing instructional structures. Rather than adding one more initiative to an already full day, educators will discover how to leverage the learning experiences they already provide to develop future-ready thinkers.

events.title: Measure What Matters: Going Beyond Raw Screen Time Data
events.original: Grayson, Sheri. Measure What Matters: Going Beyond Raw Screen Time Data. Classlink
events.description:
Counting minutes is easy; understanding what those minutes mean is harder.
With screen time now a growing concern for school boards, parents, and communities, districts need a clearer picture of how students are actually spending time online. How much of that time supports learning? What counts as productive use versus passive screen time? And how can districts respond to new screen time legislation with data instead of assumptions?
Together, we’ll look beyond raw data to understand what student screen time can reveal about learning, engagement, and digital habits. Walk away with practical insights you can use to have more informed conversations with your school board, parents, and community about how students spend their time online.

events.title: Future-Ready Schools: Leading with Foresight, Strategy, and Innovation

In this dynamic discussion, the panelists will explore real-world strategies for integrating emerging technologies, leading with agility, and building future-ready learning environments that are equitable, innovative, and sustainable.

events.title: Running the Right Plays: A District’s AI Playbook for Responsible Implementation
events.original: Harrington, Kristen. Running the Right Plays: A District’s AI Playbook for Responsible Implementation
events.description:
As AI continues to shape teaching and learning, school systems are under increasing pressure to respond quickly and often without a clear roadmap. In this session, we share our district’s journey of introducing AI with a focus on strong instructional practices, supported by a strong emphasis on digital literacy and responsible use.
Grounded in a “playbook” approach, we will reflect honestly on what worked, what didn’t, and what we would do differently. While considerations around safety, privacy, and ethics are essential, our experience has shown that decisions around AI must remain rooted in sound pedagogy and a clear focus on student learning outcomes.
Rather than focusing on specific tools, this session emphasizes sustainable, tool‑agnostic strategies that prioritize instructional integrity, student thinking, and responsible use. Participants will explore how we navigated key challenges, including staff readiness, instructional shifts, and policy considerations, while avoiding common pitfalls such as over-reliance on detection tools or reactive implementation.
Attendees will leave with practical insights, guiding principles, and a flexible framework they can use to develop or refine their own district approach to AI and ensure that innovation strengthens, rather than distracts from, effective teaching and learning.
Session Objectives
By the end of this session, participants will be able to:
Identify key challenges districts face when introducing AI, including instructional, ethical, and implementation barriers
Analyze real-world lessons learned from a district AI rollout, including missteps and course corrections
Apply a tool‑agnostic framework for evaluating and guiding AI use in teaching and learning
Shift from reactive to intentional practice by prioritizing student thinking, digital literacy, and effective instructional design
Develop next steps for building or refining a responsible, sustainable, and instructionally grounded approach to AI

events.title: AI in Special Education: Balancing Privacy, Prompt Design, and Practical Tool Mastery
events.original: Janis, Sarah. AI in Special Education. AI in Special Education: Balancing Privacy, Prompt Design, and Practical Tool Mastery
events.description:
AI can be a superpower for special educators, but navigating student data privacy and effective tool usage can feel overwhelming. This practical, example-driven session simplifies the process by contrasting two powerful AI models—Google Gemini and NotebookLM—and showing exactly how they can be used to support diverse learners and streamline administrative tasks safely.
We will begin with the absolute non-negotiable "Golden Rule" of special education AI: prioritizing confidentiality by removing Personally Identifiable Information (PII) using a reliable scrubbing and alias framework. From there, attendees will learn how to use Google Gemini for creative drafts (such as brainstorming executive function accommodations, tailoring differentiated lesson materials, and formulating SMART goals). We will then shift to NotebookLM to demonstrate how to safely ground AI in specific curriculum materials to generate things such as custom reading-level summaries, audio overviews, and guided Q&A activities tailored to unique classroom needs. Attendees will leave with practical prompt templates and a clear blueprint for ethical, high-impact AI integration.
Main Objectives:
- Master the non-negotiables of student data confidentiality by implementing a 3-step privacy framework (The Scrub, Use Aliases, and Generalized Context).
- Understand the distinct mechanics and best use-cases for a conversational assistant (Gemini) versus a grounded AI tool (NotebookLM) within a special education setting.
- Learn the anatomy of a professional prompt (Role, Task, Format, Safety) to craft effective, classroom-ready results.

events.title: Taming the SaaS Sprawl: A Strategic CTO’s Guide to Rightsizing Software and Reclaiming Funds
events.presenter: Dr. Theodore Love, Mr. Kevin Clapp
events.original: Love, Theodore. Taming the SaaS Sprawl: A Strategic CTO’s Guide to Rightsizing Software and Reclaiming Funds
events.description:
Over the past decade, the educational technology landscape has undergone a massive transformation. The era of perpetual software licenses is long gone, replaced by an overwhelming surge of Software as a Service (SaaS) applications. From assessment platforms and credit recovery systems to instructional materials and creation tools, virtually everything is now a cloud-based subscription. While this shift has brought flexibility, it has also introduced skyrocketing annual renewal costs and "SaaS sprawl," creating a major management struggle for IT directors.
In an era where Boards of Education and Superintendents face agonizing decisions—balancing critical student needs and programs against dwindling state aid and inflationary costs—the CTO must evolve from a technology manager into a strategic financial partner. Technology teams now play a crucial role in reducing overhead costs and ensuring that every dollar spent maximizes student impact.
In this highly actionable session, veteran educational leaders Kevin Clapp (former Assistant Director of the Central New York Regional Information Center at OCM BOCES) and Dr. Ted Love (who has served as Assistant Superintendent, Director of Technology, Curriculum, and People Operations) draw upon their combined 40 years of leadership experience to present a proven roadmap for SaaS management.
Presenters will share a powerful recent case study: by deploying software analysis tools to meticulously track actual application usage, and systematically reviewing that data against upcoming license renewals, they successfully optimized their district's software portfolio. Crucially, this was not done in an IT silo. The session will highlight how to develop strong, collaborative partnerships with instructional leadership to ensure that IT budgets align perfectly with instructional priorities.
The results speak for themselves: by eliminating unused or under-utilized titles and rightsizing license counts, they achieved over $70,000 in savings from a $300,000 software budget—an impressive 20% cost reduction—with minimal to no impact on students.
Attendees will leave this session equipped with:
• Frameworks for analyzing software spend and actual usage data.
• Strategies for identifying and eliminating oversubscriptions and "zombie" applications.
• Blueprints for fostering cross-departmental collaboration between IT and Curriculum & Instruction.
• A system-level approach to aligning technology resource management with ethical, data-informed decision-making.
