events.title: We Taught CS by Building Crosswalks
events.original: Thomas, Dan. We Taught CS by Building Crosswalks
events.description:
Hand students a working crosswalk and ask them to figure out how long the light should stay red. No lecture on conditionals. No vocabulary list. No flowchart of program structure. Just the problem, the physical build, and the block-based programming environment in front of them.
Watch what happens. Within twenty minutes, students are using conditional logic, variables, and timing structures — and they've named those concepts themselves because they needed them to make the light work. That's not a happy accident. That's Informed Engineering Design, and it's the pedagogical core of the NSF-funded CSED-NY project (Grant #2341962) at Hofstra University, where middle and high school Technology & Engineering teachers across the state are using authentic engineering challenges to deliver computer science content.
This session is not a project overview. It's the pedagogical argument the project is testing in twelve real classrooms: students learn CS more durably when they construct the need for the concept through a build, then reach for the vocabulary and the code as tools to solve a problem they already own. The CSED-NY curriculum — Crosswalk, Robot Arm, Robot Maze, Candy Dispenser, Treasure Chest — is the proof of concept. The principle transfers to any classroom.
Participants experience an abbreviated Crosswalk challenge as learners, then examine what just happened: which CS concepts surfaced naturally, which had to be introduced, and at what moment the introduction landed differently than a front-loaded lecture would have. From there, participants identify the "Crosswalk" inside a unit they already teach — the authentic problem that, if posed first, would make the content arrive as a tool rather than a requirement.
Objectives: (1) Experience an Informed Engineering Design sequence as a learner. (2) Identify which CS and content-area concepts students construct versus which still require direct instruction. (3) Locate the "Crosswalk" inside an existing unit — the authentic problem that makes content necessary. (4) Leave with one redesigned unit opening and an awareness of CSED-NY as a resource for T&E teachers pursuing dual CS certification.

events.presenter: Mr. Kevin Clapp, Dr. Theodore Love
events.original: Clapp, Kevin. Beyond the Network: How IT Led the Charge on Physical Security and Automated Identity Management
events.description:
In many school districts, physical security and door access control are historically managed by facilities departments, with IT brought in only as an afterthought. But what happens when IT proactively takes the lead?
Drawing on over 40 years of combined educational technology leadership experience, Kevin Clapp (former Assistant Director of the CNYRIC at OCM BOCES) and Dr. Ted Love (whose administrative experience spans Director of Technology, Director of Curriculum & Instruction, Director of People Operations, and Assistant Superintendent) present a compelling case study on transforming school safety through strategic IT integration.
This session explores how the Central Square Central School District IT department took ownership of a critical door access control project following a NYS Comptroller audit that identified physical security and card access deficiencies. Rather than applying a temporary fix, the IT team seized the opportunity to implement a system-level digital transformation.
Attendees will learn how the district partnered with an IT-focused vendor—leveraging existing unified IP telephony, emergency mass notification, and incident management systems—to build a comprehensive security ecosystem. The presentation will detail how the team conducted a complete badge access audit, cleaned up legacy records, and successfully automated staff onboarding and offboarding. By deeply integrating the physical access system with the district's primary Identity and Access Management (IAM), the IT department not only resolved network security vulnerabilities but also established a unified, automated identity management architecture.
Directly aligned with the CoSN Framework of Essential Skills (Leadership & Vision, Understanding the Educational Environment, and Managing Technology & Support Resources), this session highlights the evolving nature of modern school IT teams. Dr. Love and Mr. Clapp will share practical lessons learned in project management, cross-departmental collaboration (specifically bridging IT and Facilities), and executing effective change management with principals and district leadership. Ultimately, attendees will walk away with a blueprint for how data-informed decision-making and cross-functional leadership can result in a significant, measurable increase in the safety and security of our students.

events.title: The Power of Esports in Education: Learning Beyond the Controller
events.original: Lopez, Joel. The Power of Esports in Education: Learning Beyond the Controller. Cei.org
events.description:
Esports is one of the fastest-growing industries in the world, but its value in education extends far beyond gameplay. This session explores how CEI’s structured Esports program can serve as a powerful, standards-aligned learning environment that develops critical academic, social-emotional, and career-ready skills. Grounded in the live implementation of Esports programming in New York City schools, this presentation highlights how Esports can be leveraged to engage students and prepare them for success in college, careers, and civic life.
Participants will gain insight into the CEI Esports model, which is built on five core pillars: character, communication, teamwork, leadership, and problem-solving. These pillars are intentionally embedded into a curriculum that emphasizes life skills, character education, and college and career exploration. Through structured lessons, students are not simply playing games—they are developing transferable skills such as collaboration, resilience, decision-making, and adaptability. These experiences mirror real-world environments and align directly with the goals of the Portrait of a Graduate framework.
This session demonstrates how Esports supports durable skills by placing students in authentic, team-based scenarios where communication, strategic thinking, and accountability are essential. For example, students participate in organized tournaments, assuming roles such as team captains, referees, commentators, and analysts. These roles require leadership, problem-solving, and clear communication, helping students build confidence and agency in collaborative settings.
Technology plays a central role in enhancing student learning. By using the LMS Gameplan, educators can track student progress, monitor engagement, and provide immediate feedback. This integration of digital tools supports blended learning environments where students interact with content, reflect on their performance, and engage in continuous improvement. Additionally, students explore areas such as content creation, digital media, branding, and game development, connecting their interests in gaming to tangible technical and creative skills.
Innovation within Esports education is directly tied to career pathways. As highlighted in the presentation, Esports opens doors to fields such as digital media production, marketing, journalism, and emerging technologies. Students are introduced to these pathways through project-based learning experiences that mirror industry practices, including event management, broadcasting, and content creation. This exposure helps students envision future opportunities while developing practical skills that are applicable beyond the classroom.
A key focus of this session is empowering students as creators, collaborators, and critical thinkers. Esports provides a unique entry point for students who may not traditionally engage in school activities, allowing them to take ownership of their learning in impactful ways. Through structured competition and guided reflection, students learn how to navigate challenges, manage emotions, and grow from both success and failure. These experiences build resilience and reinforce a growth mindset, which are essential components of long-term success.
The session also addresses common misconceptions about gaming in education, reframing Esports as a purposeful, structured learning tool rather than as passive screen time. Research and classroom experience show that when implemented intentionally, Esports enhances engagement, strengthens relationships between students and staff, and creates inclusive environments that support diverse learners. Differentiated supports, including modifications for English language learners and students with disabilities, ensure that all students can access and benefit from the program.
This presentation aligns closely with the Portrait of a Graduate by developing well-rounded learners prepared to think critically, collaborate effectively, and adapt to an ever-changing world. Attendees will leave with actionable strategies, sample lesson structures, and a clear understanding of how to implement Esports in their own schools to drive engagement and meaningful learning outcomes.

events.title: Segmentation Done Right: Gaining Visibility and Control with Fortinet Network Segmentation
events.original: Ranney, Joe. Segmentation Done Right: Gaining Visibility and Control with Fortinet Network Segmentation Fortinet
events.description:
Does the lack of visibility into east-west traffic keep you up at night? Are you concerned that a compromised device could enable threat actors to move laterally throughout your district unchecked?
Fortinet Network Segmentation provides the visibility and control needed to identify and secure east-west traffic, helping prevent the spread of threats that often go undetected. By leveraging security-driven segmentation, districts can enforce granular access policies between users, devices, applications, and network segments, reducing risk and limiting lateral movement. This simple yet effective approach strengthens overall security posture while improving operational efficiency.

events.title: Blueprint for Tomorrow's Leaders
events.original: Carl Hooker. Blueprint for Tomorrow's Leaders
events.description: The future of learning isn’t something we can predict, but it is something we can help design. As AI, technology, and a rapidly changing world reshape what our students need, it’s time to take a look at our current blueprint and ask: What should we preserve? What needs to be renovated? And what are we finally ready to demolish? In this fast-paced, interactive session, Carl Hookerwill share stories, research, humor, and hands-on activities that challenge some of our assumptions about school and learning. Together, we’ll explore the human skills that matter even more in an AI-powered world and start sketching out a new blueprint for what learning (and leadership) could look like next.

events.title: From Vision to Venue: How to Run a Regional Conference

events.description: Learn how educational organizations can leverage collaboration, innovation, and strategic planning to create impactful regional conferences. Join us as we share our process for planning and scaling a regional conference, including strategies for program development, sponsor engagement, technology integration, and attendee-centered design.

events.title: Have you met my boyfriend Claude? Our Efforts to Address Mental Health in the Age of AI
events.original: Rogalski, David. Have you met my boyfriend Claude? Our Efforts to Address Mental Health in the Age of AI
events.description: The intersection of mental health and artificial intelligence is driving a profound shift in how young people seek mental health support and interpersonal connection. AI companionship is an emerging form of AI that mimics human connection and can lead to the loss of social skills, emotional dependence on AI, emotional manipulation, and the development of concerning mental health issues. Our district has recently begun wrestling with these issues, and while we are far from offering expert advice, we have begun developing a strategy to address them with students, teachers, counselors, and administrators. Join us for an interactive presentation on where we have been and where we are going.

events.title: Pass the Gravy, Not the Passwords: A Thanksgiving Feast of Edtech Solutions

events.description:
Technology leaders are often served a heaping helping of challenges: password fatigue, cybersecurity concerns, disconnected systems, and growing demands on staff and students. Join us for a fun and engaging session as we explore practical solutions that simplify access, improve security, streamline workflows, and help districts get more from their technology investments.
Whether you're looking for fresh ideas or proven strategies, you'll leave with actionable takeaways and a full plate of solutions to bring back to your district.

events.title: Beyond the Firewall: Leading the Quantum Leap from Data Protection to Data Agency
events.original: Krieger, Michelle. Beyond the Firewall: Leading the Quantum Leap from Data Protection to Data Agency
events.description:
We are all too familiar with the scenario: instructional leaders want to try the latest cutting-edge tool, while IT is forced to play the role of the 'Department of No' to keep the network safe. But as we take a 'Quantum Leap' into an AI-driven world, that separation just doesn't work anymore. Districts can't afford to choose between innovation and security. The future depends on tech governance and instructional leadership working as partners, not opposites.
This session will explore how districts transition from "check-the-box" compliance to a living "culture of data agency." Participants will leave with practical resources and materials to start this collaborative process on Monday morning.

events.title: Automate the Back Office: Workflows and AI
events.original: Duell, Nick. Automate the Back Office: Workflows and AI Droplet
events.description:
Every district has processes nobody actually designed. A hire gets approved on paper, acknowledged in one system, and tracked in a spreadsheet that one person maintains from memory. A software request sits in an inbox for a week because the person who routes it was out. Nobody built these this way on purpose. It accumulated over time, and then it became how things work.
Nick Duell, former school district IT director and now VP of Customer Experience at Droplet, has spent the last several years watching districts untangle exactly this. This session covers what separates the ones that succeed: how to choose which process to take on first, using AI to design them, and why the work continues well past go-live. The recurring examples are the ones every district recognizes, including AUP acknowledgements, field trip requests, and new hire packets. Plus, a sneak peek at the future of AI in this space: dynamic document management.

events.title: Why This Feels So Hard: Understanding Your Brain’s Social Needs at Work
events.original: Alyssa Sabbatino: Why This Feels So Hard: Understanding Your Brain’s Social Needs at Work
events.description:
Educators operate in environments that constantly activate the brain’s social threat system—through uncertainty, lack of control, shifting expectations, and relational stress. These experiences can lead to chronic stress, emotional exhaustion, and decreased capacity to respond effectively.
This session introduces the SCARF model (Status, Certainty, Autonomy, Relatedness, Fairness) as a practical framework for understanding the brain’s social needs in the workplace. Participants will identify which SCARF domains are most activated in their daily experience and explore simple, actionable strategies to regulate their responses and restore a sense of balance.
Designed for immediate application, this session offers realistic ways educators can meet their own needs—and support their students—without adding more to their workload.

events.title: Beyond the Ban: Equipping Students for a Balanced Tech Life
events.original: Girolamo, Lynn. Beyond the Ban: Equipping Students for a Balanced Tech Life
events.description: After one year of NYS’s 'bell-to-bell' smartphone ban, the critical question continues to be: what happens beyond the ban? This session moves beyond mere restriction and helps educators proactively cultivate digital wellness, fostering students' positive and intentional relationship with technology. Gain actionable strategies to ensure students build essential skills and healthy tech habits, not just follow rules. We'll explore school-wide collaboration to promote responsible tech use including the role of restorative practice to support students when they show problematic tech use. Drawing on research, we'll integrate SEL into technology, boosting empathy and digital citizenship in a post-ban world. By embracing this proactive approach to digital wellness, educators can cultivate success, well-being, and lifelong skills for students navigating today's complex digital age.

events.title: Beyond the Screen: Helping Parents Move from Fear to Framework
events.original: Keene,Becky. Beyond the Screen: Helping Parents Move from Fear to Framework
events.description: Screen time headlines are everywhere, and so is the fear. From the American Federation of Teachers calling for classroom screen bans to parent activist groups winning new restrictions in major districts, families are being told that screens and AI are simply dangerous. But not all screen time is created equal, so treating it as one undifferentiated threat leaves parents and educators without any real tool for decision-making. This session moves beyond fear, uncertainty, and doubt by giving participants a concrete framework for evaluating technology use based on intention rather than duration. Drawing on the AI Optimism Framework, we'll unpack the real difference between passive consumption and tools that build creation, connection, and critical thinking. Participants will leave with a practical, parent-friendly conversation guidance they can use immediately to navigate screen time anxiety.

events.title: The Death of the Algorithm: Reclaiming Tier 1 with Data Intimacy
events.original: Snyder, Katie. The Death of the Algorithm: Reclaiming Tier 1 with Data Intimacy
events.description:
In an era where educational "Quantum Leaps" are often measured by the speed of our automated tools, we are inadvertently losing the most powerful diagnostic engine in the classroom: the teacher’s professional intuition. As Tier 1 instruction becomes increasingly "outsourced" to automated platforms, the distance between the student’s authentic work and the teacher’s diagnostic insight continues to grow. We have more data than ever, but less "Data Intimacy." We see the syntax of a student’s work through a dashboard, but we miss the soul of their struggle.
This session is a manifesto for the intentional educator. We will challenge the "Efficiency Myth"—the idea that every automated task is a win for the teacher—and introduce **The Vitality Model**. This new framework moves beyond traditional tech models to help teachers categorize classroom actions into three zones: The Outer Ring (Scale), The Middle Ring (Visibility), and The Bullseye (Resonance). 
Participants will learn how to conduct a "Tech Autopsy" to identify which tools are "Intimacy Killers" and which are "Vitality Boosters." We will explore the "Strategic Hand-off," a workflow that delegates 80% of objective, transactional data to machines so teachers can "dominate" the 20% of transformational data that requires human empathy and professional judgment. 
By reclaiming the "slow" work of manual noticing and micro-conferencing, we don't just improve Tier 1 instruction; we model the durable skills defined in the **NYS Portrait of a Graduate**. This isn't an anti-tech session—it’s a pro-human masterclass in finding the "Sweet Spot" where technology buys back the teacher's cognitive margin, allowing them to return to the heart of the craft: knowing the student.
Main Learning Objectives
1. The Tech Audit: Participants will utilize the "Vitality Model" to audit their current classroom tech stacks, distinguishing between transactional tools (Scale) and relational tools (Soul).
2. The 80/20 Strategic Hand-Off: Attendees will design a sustainable workflow that automates rote, binary tasks (fluency, facts, compliance) to reclaim margin for manual "Data Intimacy" with high-leverage students.
3. UDL Integration: Participants will learn to apply Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles as an "Instructional Bridge," using technology to make student logic visible for deeper human evaluation.
4. Portrait of a Graduate Alignment: Educators will identify specific ways that "Data Intimacy" fosters Critical Thinking, Empathy, and Effective Communication in students by restoring teacher-student proximity.
Portrait of a Graduate Reflection
Describe how your session develops the selected Portrait of a Graduate component(s):
This session directly develops the **Critical Thinker** and **Empathetic Citizen** components of the NYS Portrait of a Graduate. 
1. Critical Thinking: By reclaiming the teacher’s cognitive margin from automated algorithms, we allow educators to model the high-level inquiry and pattern recognition that machines cannot replicate. When a teacher engages in "Data Intimacy," they are teaching students that learning is a process of logic and synthesis, not just a binary search for the "correct" answer.
2. Empathy & Communication: The Vitality Model prioritizes the "Resonance Zone"—the high-touch human feedback loop. This restores the teacher as a relational guide. By valuing the student's unique "Voice" over an auto-generated score, we foster an environment of empathy and authentic collaboration, preparing graduates for a future where human-to-human communication is the most durable skill of all. 
Innovation in this session is not defined by the *addition* of a new app, but by the *intentionality* of the human-led instruction. We empower students as creators by ensuring their creative expression is met with human validation rather than algorithmic processing.

events.title: Does your Chromebook Filter Use Advanced AI? Ours Does! Say Hello to Deledao!

New York State Technology Director (and formerly classroom teacher) Mr. Rob Zdrojewski will demonstrate how Deledao has changed the game of Chromebook filtering and classroom monitoring with their patented advanced AI capabilities not seen in our previous Chromebook filtering platform. Making the switch was seamless, and changed our philosophy of having to maintain all-or-nothing "allowed" and "blocked" lists.
Watching videos? Doing a Google image search? AI can blur images/video in REALTIME, making it possible to use sites that contain a variety of good/bad content. Plus you can give teachers the ability to handle unblock requests themselves during their class period, reducing wait time for the IT staff to take action.
This session will cover the admin and teacher aspects of Deledao, showcasing how an integrated solution that leverages AI can handle today’s evolving landscape of school filtering devices. Perfect for any OS such as Chromebooks, Windows, and iOS devices. Say goodbye to the 1990’s approach of blacklisting and whitelisting entire sites, and say hello to Deledao!
Attendees will leave this presentation knowing:
1) How artificial intelligence (patented by Deledao) changes the philosophy of web filtering on any device and OS.
2) How to leverage media detectors, game proxies, and more to dynamically filter pages as they load.
3) How to compare popular web filters such as GoGuardian and why we decided to move away from it.

events.title: Beyond the Big Wins: How Everyday Celebrations Help Students and Educators Thrive
events.original: Jezik, Carly. Beyond the Big Wins: How Everyday Celebrations Help Students and Educators Thrive
events.description:
Every day in our schools, there are moments worth celebrating: a student who takes a risk, a teacher who tries something new, a class that perseveres through a challenge, or a learner who discovers they can do something they once thought was impossible. Yet these moments are often overshadowed by the next task, goal, or expectation.
In this interactive session, participants will explore how intentional celebration can become a powerful practice for fostering well-being, resilience, and belonging in both educators and students. Through a guided Celebration Audit, attendees will reflect on their own growth and consider how small moments of recognition can create lasting ripple effects. Presenters will share personal and classroom stories, including a Writers Notebook Audit that helped students revisit a year of learning, recognize their growth, and reshape how they saw themselves as writers, alongside additional examples of how celebration and reflection can positively impact educator and student well-being.
Participants will examine how digital tools such as portfolios, reflection journals, multimedia storytelling, and collaborative platforms can help document growth, identify patterns in learning, amplify student voice, and make learning visible over time. Through artifact analysis and collaborative discussion, attendees will explore how reflection and celebration practices can support both wellness and digital fluency.
Working collaboratively, participants will engage in a Celebration Design Sprint to create a celebration and reflection experience for their own classrooms, schools, or organizations. Participants will leave with practical strategies, implementation ideas, and resources that can be immediately adapted to their learning communities.
Grounded in the idea that small shifts in perspective can lead to meaningful transformation, this session invites educators to move beyond celebrating only the big wins and instead cultivate cultures where growth, effort, joy, and progress are noticed, valued, and shared.
To conclude the session, participants will create a postcard to their future selves highlighting a meaningful accomplishment and identifying one celebration practice they commit to implementing. These postcards will be collected and mailed back to participants several weeks later, serving as a reminder that growth is often found in the small moments that shape who we become.

Directors of Technology are responsible for everything that plugs in or requires a login throughout the district. A high functioning tech department is an essential component of a successful school district, but there are currently no benchmarks, metrics or measurements for administrators to understand what is working well, what needs attention, and what is lacking within the broad spectrum of everything edtech.
The IKON EduTech Group, comprised of directors of technology with decades of experience in New York State public schools, have developed a gap analysis tool to provide school administrators a comprehensive assessment of the essential, important, and beneficial practices needed for a well-run tech department. The analysis reports will be useful in guiding directors of technology, informing superintendents, and helping new hires transition into their new position.

events.description: In an era where technology is often blamed for disconnecting young people from themselves and each other, this session flips the narrative. Participants will explore how intentional use of technology can deepen social-emotional learning, strengthen school culture, and create genuine belonging for students who are most at risk of feeling invisible. Drawing on current research and real school examples, this interactive one-hour session gives educators practical tools and strategies they can bring back to their classrooms and buildings immediately. Whether you are a classroom teacher, a counselor, a building leader, or a support staff member, you will leave with a clearer picture of how technology when used with purpose and intentionality can be one of the most powerful tools for connection we have.

events.title: Sim-Ternships: Expanding Access to Career Exploration and Work-Based Learning
events.original: Tao, Eric. Sim-Ternships: Expanding Access to Career Exploration and Work-Based Learning. MegaMinds
events.description:
Traditional career exploration often relies on career interest surveys, videos, guest speakers, and occasional workplace visits. While valuable, these approaches rarely allow students to experience the communication, decision-making, and problem-solving skills required in a career field before selecting a pathway.
This interactive session introduces the concept of "sim-ternships"—AI-powered, immersive career simulations that allow students to safely explore careers and practice workplace skills through authentic scenarios. Participants will experience examples from healthcare, skilled trades, business, and customer service while examining how simulated work-based learning can help districts expand access, reduce logistical barriers, and provide meaningful career exploration opportunities for all learners.
Attendees will leave with practical strategies for integrating simulated work-based learning into career exploration, employability skill development, and pathway selection initiatives.

events.title: Come experience this elementary ELA Lesson!
events.original: Leah Devita. Come experience this elementary ELA Lesson!
events.description:
The creation of Choose Your Own Adventure stories will engage students in collaborative digital storytelling through the creation of a “Choose Your Own Adventure” story using Google Slides. Students will practice narrative writing skills while learning how to design interactive slide presentations that allow readers to make choices that change the direction of the story and encourage re-reading. Throughout the lesson, students will work with a partner to focus on sequencing events, developing characters and plot, and using creativity to build multiple story paths. By integrating technology with literacy instruction, students will take ownership of their learning while strengthening both writing and digital communication skills.
The lesson is designed to support NYS Portrait of a Graduate attributes of Academically Prepared, Effective Communicator, and Creative Innovator by promoting engagement, collaboration, and creation as students plan and write branching storylines that connect through hyperlinks within their slides. Students will apply problem-solving skills as they determine how each decision impacts the outcome of the story, while also developing confidence using digital tools in a meaningful way. This interactive project encourages creativity, student voice, and active participation, transforming traditional storytelling into an immersive learning experience where every choice matters.

events.title: Come Experience this 8th grade STEM lesson!
events.original: Tatar, Casey. Come Experience this 8th Grade STEM Lesson.
events.description: In this interactive session, participants will step into the role of students and experience a hands-on STEM lesson centered around the Engineering Design Process. Using Sphero robots, attendees will imagine, plan, create, test, and improve a poster-sized maze or game while exploring the computational thinking and problem-solving skills that drive authentic STEM learning. Although this lesson is taught in an 8th-grade STEM classroom with a focus on robotics and coding, educators will leave with a ready-to-use project that can be easily adapted to support learning goals across content areas. Examples include reinforcing angles, measurement, coordinate geometry, or coordinate planes in mathematics; maps, geographic navigation, or historical journeys in social studies; body systems, cell structures, ecosystems, or the scientific process in science; and story elements, character journeys, sequencing, or plot development in English language arts.

events.title: The Gratitude Choir: Plug & Play Physical Computing with Makey Makey
events.original: MacWhinnie, Kaitlin. The Gratitude Choir: Plug & Play Physical Computing with Makey Makey
events.description: Give your harvest season a high-tech twist! In this hands-on workshop, discover how to transform ordinary pumpkins into an interactive, voice-recorded "Gratitude Choir" using Makey Makey and browser-based audio tools. Participants will explore core electrical concepts including conductive materials, closed vs. open circuits, and grounding while building custom harvest touch-controllers without writing a single line of code. Walk away with practical, low-prep strategies for bringing hands-on electricity concepts and physical computing into your classroom through interactive audio, quick SEL check-ins, review activities, and collaborative team-building!
